text: A Configuration Item, or CI, is ServiceNow terminology you've already brushed up against twice in this path. ITIL 4 Foundations introduced it as a practice; Platform Fundamentals named the table behind it. This lesson connects those two and gives you the real, working definition you'll use for the rest of this course.

A CI is any component of IT infrastructure — or, under the Common Service Data Model you'll meet in Chapter 3, any business or technical service or application — whose state, configuration, and relationships need tracking in order to deliver and manage services. A physical server is a CI. A specific installed application is a CI. A network switch and a database instance are CIs. The test isn't cost or whether it has a serial number — it's whether tracking it actually matters for managing services.

Here's the distinction that trips up almost every new administrator: an Incident is not a CI, and neither is a Change Request or a Problem. Those are work records on the task table — they represent something being done. A CI represents something that exists, independent of whatever work is happening to it. The two connect through a reference field: an Incident's cmdb_ci field points at the specific server or application it affects. The Incident references the CI. It is never itself a CI, and closing the Incident never touches the CI record it pointed to.

Before you model anything as a CI, ask three questions. Does it exist independent of any current work? Does its state — operational, decommissioned, upgraded — matter enough to track over time? And do its relationships, what it depends on and what depends on it, actually matter? If the answer to all three is yes, it belongs in the CMDB. If not, it's probably a plain asset, or not worth modeling at all — and getting this filter wrong early is exactly how CMDBs end up bloated with records nobody maintains.

You now have the real definition of a CI, and the one distinction that matters most: a CI is something that exists, not something being done to it. Next, you'll see how ServiceNow organizes every one of those CI types — servers, applications, network gear, databases — under a single base table, cmdb_ci, and why that hierarchy exists at all.
